quiz.explain: Ranges are start-inclusive, end-exclusive. `0..2` covers indices 0 and 1 and stops before 2 — the first two elements.

quiz.q: What kind of thing is a slice?
options: A brand-new copy of part of the collection
A borrowed view into part of a collection — it owns nothing
quiz.explain: A slice is a reference (a borrow) that views part of an existing collection. It copies nothing and owns nothing, so it can't outlive what it borrows.

options: A string slice — a borrowed view into string text
An owned, growable string on the heap
A vector of bytes you own
quiz.explain: A `&str` is a string slice: a borrowed window into text. Both text literals and slices of a String have this type.

quiz.q: You write `let piece = word[0..3];` (no `&`) on a String. Why won't it compile?
options: A slice is a borrow, so it needs the `&`
Strings can't be sliced at all
quiz.explain: A slice is a reference, so it needs `&`: `&word[0..3]`. Without it you'd be trying to move a chunk out by value, which isn't allowed.

flashcards.back: A borrowed view into part of a collection (a string or array). It copies nothing, owns nothing, and can't outlive the value it borrows from.

flashcards.front: How do you write a slice, and what does the range mean?
flashcards.back: `&thing[start..end]`. The range is start-inclusive and end-exclusive, so `[0..2]` is the first two elements (0 and 1).
A string slice — a borrowed window into text. Slicing a String gives a &str, and text literals like "hi" are also &str.

flashcards.front: What's a slice of an array called?
flashcards.back: A `&[T]` — a borrowed view over a run of elements of type T. Prefer slice parameters (&[T], &str) for read-only access.
